title: Urgent vs Routine Scheduling and Identity Verification

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish urgent, emergent, and routine appointment needs and match each to appropriate scheduling.
- Apply patient identity verification using at least two identifiers to prevent wrong-patient errors.
- Recognize red-flag symptoms and escalate urgent or emergent clinical concerns to licensed staff promptly.
- Gather and document scheduling and triage information accurately while protecting patient privacy.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Urgent is like when you cut your finger and need a bandage soon, but you are not in danger right now; you still need help today, not next month.

### Question 2

A routine visit is like a scheduled oil change for your car—you plan it ahead of time because nothing is broken right now.

### Question 3

Chest pain is like a smoke alarm going off—you do not wait to see what happens; you get help right away.

### Question 4

Verifying who someone is makes sure the doctor helps the right person—like checking a name tag before handing back the right lunchbox.

### Question 5

Using name and birthday together is like using both a first and last name to find the right person in a big class.

### Question 6

You check who someone is every single time—just like a bus driver checks each ticket on every ride, not just the first day.

### Question 7

Using a room number is like finding a student by their desk seat—when they change seats, you would get the wrong person.

### Question 8

Keeping some seats open for urgent visits is like a teacher keeping a few spots for kids who get sick and need to come in quickly.

### Question 9

The doctor decides when a patient should come back—like a coach deciding when the team should practice again.

### Question 10

Chest pain plus trouble breathing is a 'get help now' signal, like seeing fire and pulling the alarm right away.

### Question 11

The assistant is like a helpful messenger who takes an accurate note and hands it to the doctor, who then decides what to do.

### Question 12

Asking 'what is your birthday?' is like asking someone to spell their name—you let them tell you, so you do not mix them up.

### Question 13

Refilling a regular medicine is like topping off a monthly prescription—nothing is broken, so it goes through the normal process.

### Question 14

You double-check the name before doing anything, like checking a nametag before putting the right test in the right folder.

### Question 15

It is like making sure the person at the door is who they say they are before handing over a private letter.

### Question 16

A sudden, terrible headache is like a loud alarm—it means something serious might be wrong, so you get help fast.

### Question 17

Urgent means 'soon, not right this second'—so you find a spot today or tomorrow instead of next month.

### Question 18

Scheduling acuity is like sorting kids into lines—the ones who need help right away get seen first, and everyone else gets a fair turn.

### Question 19

When two kids have the same name, you check their birthdays to tell them apart—same idea for patients.

### Question 20

If the name tag and the folder do not match, you stop and double-check before anything else—never just keep going.

### Question 21

Emergent is 'call 911 now,' like a fire; urgent is 'see a doctor today,' like a bad sprain.

### Question 22

Two checks are safer than one—like needing both a key and a code to open a special door.

### Question 23

The assistant asks the parent what is wrong, writes it down carefully, and hands it to the nurse or doctor—just like taking a message.

### Question 24

Putting the right name on the right file means the doctor's notes and test results go to the right person.

### Question 25

When you are not sure if something is dangerous, you ask an adult—or in this case, the nurse or doctor.

### Question 26

Slurred speech and one-sided weakness are like a flashing red light—get emergency help right away.

### Question 27

A yearly checkup with no new problems is a routine visit, while new chest pain or confusion are 'get help now' situations.

### Question 28

If a usually clear-thinking grandparent suddenly gets very confused, that is a 'tell the doctor right away' signal.

### Question 29

A fever in a tiny baby is a big deal—get the doctor involved right away, just like calling for help when a baby seems sick.

### Question 30

When someone cannot explain what is wrong, you ask gentle questions to figure it out, and if you are still worried, you get a grown-up's help.

### Question 31

You check the name and birthday before collecting, then write the right name on the tube—like labeling your own water bottle so it does not get mixed up.

### Question 32

You do not hand over a private report until you are sure you are talking to the right person.

### Question 33

Letting the person say their own birthday is like letting them spell their own name—you find mistakes instead of covering them up.

### Question 34

It is like always checking your name on the attendance list—it keeps everyone safe, even if it feels repetitive.

### Question 35

A yearly checkup is planned ahead of time, like booking a dentist cleaning—you pick a day that works for everyone.

### Question 36

Chest pain plus sweating and trouble breathing is a 'call for help right now' situation, like seeing smoke and flames together.

### Question 37

When someone is scared, you listen and help—you never just wave them away.

### Question 38

Most refills are ordinary, but a few special medicines need the doctor's quick attention—like most mail being regular but some letters needing a signature.

### Question 39

The assistant is a careful lookout who raises the alarm and hands over the details—not the one who decides the final plan.

### Question 40

If someone feels like they might faint, help them sit down safely and get a grown-up to help right away.

### Question 41

You find the right way to talk to each person—like using pictures or a translator—so everyone is helped fairly and safely.

### Question 42

A room number is like a seat number—when someone moves seats, the old number belongs to someone else.

### Question 43

Writing down what happened is like taking good notes in class so nothing important is forgotten later.

### Question 44

Someone who cannot be woken or cannot breathe is a 'call 911 now' emergency.

### Question 45

Suddenly not being able to see out of one eye is a big warning sign—tell the doctor right away.

### Question 46

If someone says they might hurt themselves, you stay with them and get help right away—never leave them alone.

### Question 47

A swollen throat and trouble breathing after a sting is like a very fast, serious emergency—get help immediately.

### Question 48

If the usual medicine is not helping someone breathe, it is time to get the doctor involved right away.

### Question 49

Writing things down means the next helper knows exactly what happened, like leaving a clear note for a teammate.

### Question 50

If you skip checking who someone is, the wrong person might get the wrong medicine or the wrong test—that is dangerous.

### Question 51

If a name is spelled wrong, you double-check who the person is and fix it carefully instead of starting a whole new file.

### Question 52

When someone's name changes, you check their birthday to confirm it is still them, then update the name the right way.

### Question 53

A wristband is like a name tag you check every time before helping, so you help the right person.

### Question 54

For a baby or child, you check the child's name and birthday and make sure the grown-up with them is allowed to be there.

### Question 55

Even if you think you know someone, you still check their nametag—that keeps everyone safe.

### Question 56

If someone might have broken a bone, you get them in to be checked the same day, not next month.

### Question 57

The doctor needs to know when the problem started, how bad it is, and if anything else is wrong—like clues for solving a puzzle.

### Question 58

When you are not sure what to do, you ask the person in charge instead of guessing.

### Question 59

You kindly explain which times are available, like a librarian helping someone find an open time for a study room.

### Question 60

You only share private information with someone who is allowed to have it—like only giving a key to people on the approved list.

### Question 61

The person who might be having a heart problem goes first—like letting the most hurt person skip the line.

### Question 62

If someone's face droops or they cannot lift an arm or speak clearly, call for emergency help right now.

### Question 63

A problem that appears all at once is usually more serious than one that creeps in slowly over weeks.

### Question 64

Lots of people are named 'Jordan,' but 'Jordan born on July 3' is much easier to tell apart from others.

### Question 65

When the doctor says 'come back in two weeks,' you book the appointment for about two weeks—not next year.

### Question 66

If someone cannot remember their birthday, you find another safe way to confirm who they are and let the nurse know, because confusion can be a sign of illness.

### Question 67

Checking who someone is before sharing private health details is like checking an ID before handing over a private package.

### Question 68

The person who might be having a stroke goes first—like the fire engine getting through traffic before other cars.

### Question 69

Even if someone thinks their chest pain is just heartburn, you still get help, because chest pain can be a heart problem in disguise.

### Question 70

When two folders look almost identical, you look for a special ID number to tell them apart—like checking a locker number, not just a name.

### Question 71

If two folders do not match, you stop and sort it out the right way before using either one.

### Question 72

You confirm who is calling first, then share only the smallest amount of private information needed to help—like checking an ID before showing one page, not the whole book.

### Question 73

The most serious problem goes first—like the emergency crew helping the worst injury before the small scrapes.

### Question 74

You only hand over private papers to someone who is officially allowed to have them, like checking the authorized pickup list.

### Question 75

When clues are unclear, you gather what you can and ask an expert instead of guessing the answer yourself.

### Question 76

After a hospital visit, the instructions say when to come back—you book that visit for the right person at the right time.

### Question 77

Deciding how sick someone is is the doctor's or nurse's job—the assistant passes along the clues instead of guessing the answer.

### Question 78

If the birthday does not match, you stop and double-check—never just keep going with the wrong folder.

### Question 79

You make room for the kid who needs help right now, even if the class is full—but only when it is truly needed.

### Question 80

Emergent is 'call 911 now'; urgent is 'see a doctor today or tomorrow'—different problems, different speed of help.

### Question 81

A sudden 'worst headache ever' is a loud warning—get help right away, not later.

### Question 82

Getting the right person first is like putting the first piece of a puzzle in place—everything else only works if that first piece is right.

### Question 83

Catching the wrong folder before the doctor acts is a good save—now you stop, get the right one, and tell the team so it does not happen again.

### Question 84

Even when you are in a hurry, you still check every nametag—because rushing is when mistakes sneak in.

### Question 85

After telling the doctor, you write down what happened so there is a clear record—like leaving a note for the next person on the team.
